activity: going on a first date
story:
Stella changed her shirt three times before Cheyenne texted that she was outside, and by then the bedroom floor looked like a small explosion had happened in a thrift store. "It's bowling," Cheyenne said through the window of her car, "not a job interview." Stella got in with the blue shirt, the safe one, and Ms. Siddiqui from next door was watering her mums on the porch as they pulled away, which meant Stella would have to hear about the date tomorrow over the fence, probably in more detail than she wanted to give.

The boy was called Brodie, and he was in her English class, and he had lent her his notes the week she had the flu, notes she had sat at the kitchen table transcribing into her own handwriting because his abbreviations were so strange and precise they felt like a secret code. He had a nice laugh. That was the fact she kept returning to, the one solid thing. Everything else about the evening was guesswork, and she was, if she was honest, a person who liked fewer guesses.

The bowling alley smelled like rented shoes and blue slushie syrup. They ended up tied going into the tenth frame, which neither of them had planned, and Brodie suggested a tiebreaker, sudden death, one roll each. Stella's first ball clipped the ten pin and left a wobbly seven standing, and Brodie needed only eight pins to win. She watched him line up his shot with the concentration of someone defusing something, and her heart was going so hard she could feel it in her ears.

He got nine. He won. He turned around with his fists up like he'd taken a title, and something in Stella's chest did a movement she could not immediately classify. It was somewhere between the feeling of a near-miss on the highway and the feeling of being handed a gift she hadn't asked for. Brodie sat down next to her on the scratched plastic bench, close, still laughing, and the jittery thing kept going, her hands actually trembling a little around her slushie straw.

Here was the problem, and it interested her enough to forget to be awkward. Was the jittery feeling about Brodie, or was it just the tiebreaker? She had read something months ago, late at night in one of those internet spirals, and it surfaced now like a coin from the bottom of a pool. Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement is mistaken for attraction to the person nearby. She turned the phrase over while Brodie told a story about his uncle's league trophies. So which was it? How would a person even check? You couldn't exactly run a controlled experiment on yourself in a bowling alley, though the idea of trying made her want to laugh.

She tried, quietly, the way she tried things. She let her breathing slow and watched him when nothing was happening, between frames, when the score screen showed an advertisement for laser tag. Nothing particular occurred in her chest. Then the screen flashed and the alley lights dimmed for cosmic bowling, and her heart rate climbed on schedule, purple and strobing, and she thought: so the machinery is jumpy tonight regardless. Which proved nothing either way, and she knew it. A quiet heart between frames didn't mean there was no crush, any more than a loud one during a tiebreaker meant there was. Feelings, unlike lab results, refused to be transcribed cleanly.

Outside, under the buzzing parking lot light, Brodie asked if she wanted to do this again and she said yes, and she meant it, and she also noticed that she did not know why she meant it, and that not knowing felt less like a failure than it would have a year ago. Even Cheyenne, who had strong opinions about everything from existentialism to which cafeteria line moved fastest, had admitted once that some things stayed murky. "Murky isn't the same as bad," Cheyenne had said, eating fries on Stella's back steps. "Murky just means you're still collecting data." Stella wasn't sure she'd agree that a person was data, exactly, but the murkiness, at least, she could agree to sit with.

At home, late, Ms. Siddiqui's kitchen light was still on, a yellow rectangle in the dark, and there was a text from Brodie with a single bowling pin emoji and the question, did you have fun? Stella stood in the hallway holding her phone, her heart doing its small steady work, telling her nothing except that she was alive and seventeen and that tomorrow she would get to find out a little more. She typed, I did, honestly. Then she sat down on the stairs to decide about the emoji.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
story:
The computer cabin smelled of pine sap and overheated laptops, and by the second week of camp Mr. McKenzie had posted the challenge on the corkboard: hidden somewhere in a list of two hundred and twelve camper names was a single marked name, and whichever pair found it in the fewest steps would get out of dish duty for the rest of the summer. Kayla wanted that. She had scrubbed the industrial pot twice already, and the gray water had a way of coagulating around the drain that made her think the pot itself was giving up on being clean.

Daniel claimed he already had the answer. "Binary search," he said on the dock that evening, kicking his sandals against the wood while Romane fed crumbs to a doubtful duck. "You take the middle name, compare it to the one you want, and throw away the half of the list that can't contain it. Two hundred names, and you only look at a handful." He said it with the flat certainty of someone repeating an aphorism he'd heard once and never tested, and Kayla, who trusted methods less than she trusted results, said nothing. She planned to start at the top of the list and read every name until she found the marked one. It was slow, but it could not lie to her.

Mr. McKenzie handed out the printed lists the next morning. He was choleric before coffee, waving the stapled pages like warrants, and he gave them exactly one hour. Kayla and Romane sat on the floor near the window and began at the first line. Abernathy, Achebe, Adams. Romane read aloud while Kayla tracked the count on her fingers, and across the cabin Daniel was folding his list into halves with a showman's flourish, then quarters, tapping a pen at each middle name and slicing away whole sections of paper with scissors he had brought for the purpose. It looked like magic. It looked like the future. Kayla kept reading.

Forty minutes in, they had reached the R's. Romane's voice had gone thin. Meanwhile Daniel stood up, scowling, holding a list that had been reduced to confetti. "It's not there," he announced, too loudly. "The marked name isn't in the list at all. Someone should check McKenzie's data." Mr. McKenzie's neck went the color of the camp flag. "The name is in the list," he said, each word bitten off separately. "I put it there myself."

Kayla stopped reading. She looked at Daniel's wreckage of paper strips on the floor, and she noticed something she would not be able to explain until later: the strips did not go in order. A strip beginning with K lay on top of one beginning with C. She picked up the original list, untouched on her own clipboard, and ran her eye down the left margin, and the truth arrived slowly, the way cold water arrives through a sneaker. The list was not sorted. Names wandered out of sequence every few lines, Blythe after Brennan, Osei before O'Donnell, as though whoever had typed it had simply stopped caring halfway through.

She said it out loud, quietly, mostly to herself. "Binary search only works on sorted data." Daniel heard her anyway. He looked at his shredded pile, then at the floor, and the showman's flourish went out of him entirely. "It compares the target with the middle item," Kayla went on, almost apologizing, "and throws away the half that can't contain it. But if the list isn't sorted, you can't know which half that is. You might throw away the half with your name in it." Romane, still holding their page at the R's, looked at the clock. Twenty minutes left.

They moved fast. Romane read the names aloud in rough order and Kayla wrote them into a fresh list, alphabetized by hand, crossing off and inserting while the other cabins' footsteps passed the window on their way to lunch. When the new list was sorted, Kayla folded it Daniel's way, out of respect or irony or both. She took the middle item, compared it to the marked name she wanted, discarded the half that could not contain it, and did it again. Seven comparisons. The marked name was Vasseur, Claire, sitting three-quarters of the way down the original list, in a stretch that Romane's tired voice would not have reached for another ten minutes.

They brought the sorted list and the marked name to Mr. McKenzie, who verified it, and the cabin next door cheered through the wall. Romane hugged Kayla so hard the clipboard cracked. That evening, freed from the dish pit, Kayla carried two root beers down to the dock, where Daniel sat alone with his laptop, rebuilding something. She held one out to him. He took it, and opened his mouth to say the thing people say about luck and fairness, and she waited to hear which version he'd chosen. Behind them the kitchen door banged open and Romane shouted across the darkening water, "Kayla, McKenzie says congratulations, you're on pot duty anyway. Everyone else quit."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
story:
Sierra arrived at the book club with the novel under her arm and a notebook full of nothing, which was a problem, because she had promised Ms. Adeyemi she would lead the discussion tonight. She had promised this three weeks ago, back when The Great Gatsby was still a book she intended to read twice. Instead she had read it once, fast, on the bus, and had formed exactly one opinion, which was that she liked the green light and distrusted everything else.

The meeting was in the back room of the bookshop, where the heater rattled like something trying to escape. Lina was already there, arranging biscuits into a fan shape as though the biscuits required presentation. Jack sat with his feet on a second chair, and Ms. Adeyemi, who ran the club and owned the shop, was stamping a stack of used paperbacks at the corner table.

"Right," Sierra said, once everyone had tea. "So. Nick Carraway."

"Thrilling opener," said Lina. "Really grabs a reader."

"I'm building suspense." Sierra flipped her notebook open to the blank page, which Lina could clearly see, because Lina leaned over and tapped it. "You have one opinion and zero notes."

"One opinion and two notes," Sierra said, and wrote, to make it true, one and two.

Jack said he liked Nick because Nick was normal. "Everyone else in the book is running around having parties and pretending to be somebody, and Nick just watches. He's the camera."

Sierra had thought that too, on the bus. It was a comfortable thought. The problem was that it had started to bother her, the way a pebble bothers you in a shoe, small and positional, and she couldn't say why.

Then Ms. Adeyemi, without looking up from her stamping, said, "Oh, I love that line of his. Near the end. 'I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known.'"

"The book was published in 1925," Lina said, "and that is still the most confident thing anyone has ever said about themselves."

Everyone laughed, and Sierra laughed too, and then stopped, because something seismic happened in her head, or at least something that felt seismic to a girl with one opinion. Nick claimed to be honest. And she had believed him, instantly, on the bus, the way you believe the first person to speak in a room.

"Wait," she said. "Is he, though?"

Jack frowned. "He's the narrator. He's telling us everything."

"Is he, though," Sierra said again, and pulled the book toward her, and started hunting. The heater rattled. Lina ate a biscuit in a deliberately annoying way, crunching with her eyes closed.

"He doesn't tell Daisy that Gatsby's money comes from bootlegging," Sierra said, flipping pages. "He doesn't tell Tom that Daisy was driving the car. He skips the whole thing where he supposedly breaks up with his girlfriend back home, and he calls himself careless about her while calling everyone else careless. He gets drunk on his thirtieth birthday and leaves a whole scene out." She looked up. "He's honest about other people's lies. His own, he compartmentalizes. There's a drawer for those."

"That's a system," said Lina. "I respect a man with filing."

"But here's what I can't decide," Sierra said, and she meant it, this was the pebble, this was the actual problem. "I trusted him anyway. All the way through. So is that my fault or the book's? Like, did it trick me, or did I want to be tricked?"

Jack said that was too big a question for a room with a rattling heater. Lina said that was exactly the right size of question for a room with a rattling heater. Ms. Adeyemi set her stamp down at last and said only, "Go on," which was not an answer, and Sierra understood it was not meant to be.

She stood up and drew two boxes on the whiteboard, one labeled ME and one labeled NICK, with an arrow looping between them. "It's not a trick exactly. It's more like a symbiosis. He needs me to trust him so his version becomes the only version, and I need someone to trust so the story has a floor to stand on. We're both getting something out of the arrangement." She tapped the arrow. "The question is whether I can notice the arrangement while I'm inside it. And I don't know. I noticed it tonight, but tonight I had all of you, and on the bus I just had me."

"Add a third box," Lina said. "LINA."

"Add a fourth," said Jack. "The heater. The heater saw everything."

Ms. Adeyemi said the shop closed at nine, and that the next meeting was in two weeks, and that Sierra could pick the book. Sierra looked at her two boxes and her looping arrow, still uncertain, still somehow pleased, and said, "Something with a narrator who lies less. Or more. I haven't decided which would be harder." Lina put the last biscuit in Sierra's tea, whole, and watched it float.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
story:
Nathan considered himself, without evidence, a natural in the kitchen. He had watched perhaps forty cooking videos at double speed and had once made scrambled eggs so good that Matt asked for seconds, which Nathan mentioned at least weekly. So when his dad's furlough stretched into its second month and the family started eating like siege survivors, Nathan volunteered to take over dinner. He announced this at the restaurant where he washed dishes on Saturdays, leaning on the steel counter while Mr. Ahmadi inspected a delivery of onions.

"You will plan first," Mr. Ahmadi said. "Seven dinners. One shopping list. You cook twice, in batches, and you freeze what you will not eat in three days. This is how a kitchen survives." Nathan nodded as though he had already internalized all of this, which he had not, but nodding felt like progress.

Trinity came along on the shopping trip because she claimed he would otherwise buy six kinds of chips and call it a cuisine. At the store she wrestled the list from him when he tried to add a "surprise aisle item," and she made him put back a novelty hot sauce shaped like a fire extinguisher. "Your family is eating on a budget," she said. "The only surprise should be that dinner exists." They bought chicken thighs, two bags of dried beans, carrots going soft at a discount, a sad but dignified cabbage, and rice in a quantity that made the cashier say wow.

Sunday he cooked. The restaurant training held up better than expected: he browned the chicken properly, salted the beans with something close to courage, and produced a stew and a tray of roasted everything. He portioned it into containers and, following his own genius rather than any instruction, stacked the lids slightly ajar so nothing would, in his words, "suffocate." Matt, who had come over to eat and mostly to watch, said that looked wrong. Nathan said air was natural. Matt ate a second helping and stopped arguing.

Wednesday the beans. Thursday the roast vegetables, slightly glazed with something sweet that he chose not to investigate. By Friday, with his dad working a shift swap and his mom late, Nathan opened the container marked STEW and found the surface patchy and white, dry-looking, like frost that had given up. He stood at the counter holding it the way you hold a failing grade.

Matt picked him up for the Saturday shift, took one look at the container Nathan had brought in a cooler like evidence, and called Trinity from the car. She was no help. "It's freezer burn," she said. "My mom throws it out." Nathan, who had secretly hoped for a chemistry problem with a chemistry answer, said nothing. At the restaurant he carried the container to the back and set it, casually, on the prep table where Mr. Ahmadi could not miss it.

Mr. Ahmadi did not miss it. He turned the container in his hands, tapped the pale patch with a spoon, and said, "Freezer burn. The air got in and dried the surface." Nathan confessed the ajar-lid system. "It makes the food tough and tasteless," Mr. Ahmadi went on, spooning a little onto a plate, "but it will not make you sick. It is safe to eat. It is only a disappointment." He tasted it, chewed with the patience of a man grading a pap smear, and said the stew had earned its punishment, but the technique underneath was sound. Nathan felt this was roughly half a compliment and took the whole thing.

So Nathan made a second batch that night after his shift, and this time he pressed the lids down until they clicked, expelled the stew's enemies, wrote the dates on masking tape like a person with a system. He carried the new containers home in the cooler, reheated one portion for his parents, and stood by the table waiting for the verdict with his arms crossed like a man owed a trophy.

His dad took a bite, then another, then pushed his chair back and looked at his son with what Nathan chose to read as awe. "This is the best thing you've made," his dad said. "What's the recipe?"

"It's the same stew," Nathan said. "From last week. I just fixed the lids."

His dad set down the fork. "So the white stuff was on this?"

"Was," Nathan said. "Before I scraped it."

His mom laughed so hard she had to leave the table, and his dad, slowly, picked the fork back up.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
story:
Edouard sat in the driver's seat of his mother's old hatchback with his hands at ten and two, exactly where the booklet said, while Ms. Do folded herself into the passenger side and set her coffee in the cup holder like she had done this a thousand times. The driveway was long and gravelled, bordered by a hedge his father trimmed every second Saturday, and at the end of it the road ran past a faded speed sign that some kid had shot at with a pellet gun years ago.

"Mirror, signal, shoulder check," Ms. Do said. "Then roll out when it's clear." She said it the way people say things they've said so often the words have gone smooth. Edouard had spent the whole week torn between two philosophies he couldn't name: his mother's, which held that a car was a weapon and every trip was a negotiation with death, and his uncle's, which held that driving was simply competence, a skill like soldering, to be learned and then trusted. He wanted to believe the second one and could not stop hearing the first.

He checked the mirror, signalled, looked over his shoulder, and pulled out. The car lurched, stalled, lurched again. Ms. Do sipped her coffee without comment, which he decided was either patience or indifference, and he couldn't tell which bothered him more.

They drove the loop past the school and the shuttered garden centre. Kyan had texted him that morning, nonchalant about it, saying his own instructor had been a screamer and that Edouard should count himself lucky. Edouard wasn't sure luck had anything to do with anything lately. He kept creeping up behind the cars ahead of him, his foot unsure how much pressure meant what, until he was close enough to read the bumper stickers on a Corolla, and Ms. Do said, "You're crowding him. Back off a touch."

"How far back?" He was genuinely asking. Distance in metres meant nothing to him yet; he had no feel for it.

"Watch the sign coming up," she said. "When his rear bumper passes it, count. You want to reach that sign no sooner than two seconds after he does. That's the two-second rule."

Edouard watched the shot-up speed sign slide toward them. The Corolla's bumper crossed it, and he counted, one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand, and his own hood crossed it before he got to the end of the second count. So that was what too close looked like, translated into time instead of distance. It was strange to him that something spatial could be measured by counting, as if the road had been secretly temporal all along. He eased off the gas and tried again at the next lamppost, and this time he made it to two. Something in his shoulders let go.

They practised it the whole way back. Ms. Do never explained it twice, never turned it into a lecture; she just let him find the rhythm, and he found himself wondering whether that was what good teaching was, not the transferring of a rule but the leaving of a space where a person could arrive at it. His uncle would have called her an iconoclast for not drilling him, though Edouard suspected the word didn't quite fit, that she was more like someone who had simply seen a hundred students and knew which ones needed talking and which ones needed quiet. Or maybe that was the same thing.

Turning back into the driveway, he overcooked it and rolled a wheel onto the gravel edge, the stones cracking under the tyre. Ms. Do laughed, a short unguarded sound. "Better than my first lesson," she said. "I hit a hedge."

He parked crooked but complete, engine ticking as it cooled, and sat there with his hands still at ten and two. He hadn't decided, he realized, whether the car was a weapon or a tool, and he wasn't going to decide today; what he had instead was a way of counting, a sign at the end of the driveway, and the thought that some questions you hold the way you hold a steering wheel, lightly, with both hands, eyes moving. He looked down the drive toward the shot-up sign and started counting, just to see how long two seconds felt from a standing stop.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
story:
The trail behind the school cut along a ridge and then dropped toward the pond, and Mason had spread his flashcards on the bench at the halfway point because he refused to fail the retake twice. Jawad sat on the bench's armrest, bouncing a lacrosse ball against his sneaker. Frederique stood at the rail over the water, reading the backs of the cards Mason had dealt her like a dealer at a casino, flicking them back one by one when he got them wrong.

"Glycolysis," she said.

"Glucose gets split. In the cytoplasm, not the mitochondria. That's the trick question."

"Correct. Krebs cycle."

"It's in the mitochondrial matrix and I don't know what comes out of it, exactly. A bunch of things. Carriers." He heard how it sounded, vague, a guess dressed up as an answer, and Jawad grinned without looking up from his ball.

"You're cooked," Jawad said.

"I'm not cooked. Mr. Bighorn said if I get the overall picture right, the steps can be fuzzy." It wasn't exactly what Mr. Bighorn had said. What Mr. Bighorn had said, leaning on the doorframe after class with his thermos, was that Mason memorized lists the way other kids forgot them, instantly and in order, and that maybe he needed one true thing to hang everything else on. Mason had liked that advice without trusting it. Advice was a heuristic at best, a shortcut that worked until the terrain changed, and the terrain had changed last Thursday when he'd opened the exam and gone blank in the first five minutes.

Frederique flicked a card back at him. "This one you missed twice already."

"Electron transport chain."

"Where?"

"Inner membrane of the mitochondria. The folded part. Cristae." He said the word carefully, the way he'd practiced it, and she nodded once, unimpressed, because nodding was all the ceremony she ever offered.

The afternoon had gone cold while they climbed, and the pond below the rail was flat and gray, ringed with cattails bent from the wind. Mason's breath came out in clouds. He watched one drift and thin and vanish over the water, and something about it snagged on the card still face down in Frederique's hand. He took the card from her, turned it over, and read the back to himself instead of aloud. The overall equation. He'd copied it off the board Tuesday, C6H12O6 plus 6 O2 yields 6 CO2 plus 6 H2O plus energy, and he'd said it to himself on the bus like a rhyme without ever once wondering what it was describing.

"That cloud," he said. "My breath. Where's the carbon in it from?"

Jawad stopped bouncing the ball. "From, like, your lungs? You just breathe out whatever's in there."

"No, but where did it come from before it was in my lungs? It came from food. Glucose. It's in the equation, look." He held the card up as if Jawad could read it at that distance. "Glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water. The glucose I ate for lunch, the oxygen I just breathed in, and this." He exhaled deliberately, a long slow cloud that hung above the rail. "That's me leaking out the products of the reaction. Six carbons in a glucose, six CO2 coming out of me. I'm literally exhaling my breakfast."

"That's disgusting," Frederique said, but she leaned in to look at the card.

"It's the overall equation. That's the one true thing. Everything else, glycolysis, Krebs, the transport chain, they're all just the route the carbon takes from breakfast to that cloud. It's like the trail." He pointed down the ridge, at the path switchbacking through the oaks toward the water. "You can walk it step by step or you can say you started at the top and ended at the pond. Both are true. One of them you can memorize in a night."

"So the mitochondria," Frederique said, testing him, and Mason found that for once the question didn't empty him out. The mitochondria were the second half of the walk. Glucose gets split outside, in the cytoplasm, and the pieces go in, and inside, in the matrix and then along the inner membrane, the rest of the energy comes loose, packaged as ATP. The carbon left over went to CO2 and out through his blood, his lungs, the cold air over the pond. He could still get the order of the carriers wrong. He would probably still get the carriers wrong. But the wrongness would be an auxiliary detail now, something hanging off a structure, not the whole structure gone missing.

Jawad threw the ball against a tree trunk, caught it on the rebound. "So when I run sprints and I'm dying, that's glucose and oxygen turning into CO2 and water in me?"

"Six of each," Mason said. "Six O2 in, six CO2 out, per glucose. It's on the card."

"And the water part?"

"Also a product. Six waters." He looked at the pond again, at all that water, at the geese standing in the shallows on their thin legs, and a question opened in him that he decided not to close: whether the pond and his breath and the sandwich in his pack were one ledger being balanced, or whether that was just a pretty way of talking that would fall apart the moment he tried to take it further. He couldn't tell yet. Mr. Bighorn would probably say both.

Frederique squared the cards and handed them back. "Run it once more. Whole thing, top to bottom."

Mason stood, took a breath, and started at the top of the ridge, saying glucose, and walked the switchbacks down toward the water with the cards in his back pocket, telling the trail where each step happened, Jawad lobbing the ball ahead of him the whole way down.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
story:
Raphael's grandmother kept a photograph on the fridge of his grandfather holding up his left thumb, the nail stained a brownish purple, grinning like a man who had just won something. He had asked her about it once when he was small, and she had said, "Election day, Bangalore," and gone back to her tea, and he had filed it under things that belonged to her world, not his.

Now he was eighteen, and the election belonged to him too. The community hall on Fairview Road had been a badminton court in a previous life; the nets were gone but the lines remained under folding tables and a queue that moved at a glacial pace. His father had dropped him off with a nod that carried more weight than it should have, as if the act were being witnessed by generations of people who had not been permitted it. Raphael did not want that inheritance imputed to him so easily. He had not studied the candidates the way Harrison had, with spreadsheets and a podcast in his earbuds for six weeks. He had studied them the way you study weather, knowing you would have to walk out into whatever arrived.

Harrison was already inside, standing near the coffee urn that nobody was allowed to plug in. "I voted at seven a.m.," he said. "I've been waiting for you to see if you did the right thing."

"I haven't decided what the right thing is."

"Oh God." Harrison rubbed his face. "There are two serious candidates. One of them is a landlord who calls public transit a subsidy for people who failed. The other one actually shows up to council meetings. This is not a philosophy seminar."

"It's a little bit a philosophy seminar. If the landlord wins, the developers win, and the developers already own half the council. That's just an oligarchy with paperwork."

"See, this is why Jaeden refuses to eat lunch with you."

Jaeden came in from the parking lot, hood up despite the mild morning, and got in line behind Raphael without ceremony. He was voting for the landlord, which he had announced at lunch on Thursday with the flat pleasure of someone who enjoys being contrarian. "He'll lower my dad's commercial rent," Jaeden said now, before anyone asked. "The other guy talks about affordability like it's a religion."

The line advanced one voter. A woman with a toddler on her hip let the toddler push the pen across the registration sheet, then corrected the resulting squiggle. Ms. Do, who had taught all three of them civics in grade ten, was working the table as a deputy returning officer, her reading glasses low on her nose, initialing forms with terrible efficiency. When Raphael reached her, she looked up.

"Raphael. Congratulations."

"It's just a municipal election."

"It's never just anything to the person doing it for the first time." She turned his voter card over, checked the back, and stamped something. "There's a mark on your card. If someone tried to use your name twice, the system would catch it here."

He thought of the photograph then, suddenly and completely, the stained thumb on the fridge. "My grandfather used to come home from voting with ink on his finger," he said. "In India. It wouldn't wash off for days."

"Silver nitrate," Ms. Do said, without looking up. "They've marked fingers with indelible ink since the 1962 general election, so no one can vote twice." She handed him his ballot. "Every country solves the problem differently."

He stood in the booth longer than he meant to, pencil hovering. The landlord's name sat at the top of the list, printed first, which itself felt like a small advantage nobody had voted for. He thought about Jaeden's father's rent, which was real, and about Harrison's spreadsheets, which were also real, and about his grandfather's thumb, purple for days, a mark you carried out of the polling station into the street where everyone could see what you had done. There was no mark here. You folded your ballot and it disappeared into a box and nobody could ever prove you had been part of it. He understood, in the cramped booth, that he was trying to hold two things at once: the vote as a private calculation of interest, and the vote as a public act, a thing you showed your finger for. He could not make them fully agree. He wrote the name of the candidate who attended the meetings, then stood for a moment longer, honest with himself that he was not certain, that the certainty belonged to people like Harrison and Jaeden, and that perhaps uncertainty was the tax on trying to see both sides at all.

Outside, Harrison was waiting on the steps. "Well?"

"I'll tell you in four years whether it was right."

Jaeden laughed from below, hood still up, already walking toward the bus stop. "He's not going to tell you even then." Raphael looked at his own clean fingers, then put his hands in his pockets and followed.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
story:
The screen door at her grandmother's house still stuck in the same place, halfway, and Brooklyn lifted it by the frame the way she had since she was nine. She carried her laptop bag past the kitchen, where her grandmother was sorting beans at the table, and out to the back porch, where the afternoon came through the pecan tree in moving coins of light. Ms. Adebayo had assigned a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question, and Brooklyn had chosen hers too fast, in the library on Tuesday, mostly because they seemed to disagree and disagreement looked like an easy structure. She had not read either one closely yet. That was the trouble.

The question she had picked was whether later school start times improved adolescent sleep, which felt almost comically personal, since she was doing this work on a Saturday. She read the first article slowly, marking its argument the way Ms. Adebayo had shown them, claim and then evidence and then the limits of the evidence. It was careful to the point of dullness. Its conclusion was so pithy she copied it onto the back of a grocery receipt: modest gains, heterogeneous samples, more research needed. The second article was livelier. It claimed large effects, cited itself confidently, and swept through six studies in three pages. She liked it more, and distrusted herself for liking it.

Her grandmother came out with a glass of lemonade and set it down without asking whether she wanted it. "You're doing homework at my house now," she said. "That's new." Brooklyn said the library was loud, which was only half true; the house was quiet in a way her apartment never managed. Her grandmother sat in the other chair and went back to her beans even out here, a bowl balanced on her knee, sorting through them with one hand. Brooklyn scrolled to the references of the second article and noticed something she had skimmed past twice before: it had never appeared in a journal. There was no volume, no issue, only a server name and a posting date, and the words "not yet peer reviewed" printed plainly at the top, which she had somehow read and not read.

She texted Charly, who answered homework questions faster on Saturdays than anyone had a right to. "It's a preprint," Charly wrote back, before Brooklyn had even finished describing it. Brooklyn typed "meaning what" and then deleted it, because the page had already told her, in its own small print: a paper posted publicly before peer review, its findings not yet checked by independent experts chosen by a journal. Charly sent a follow-up anyway: "you can use it, just say what it is." Then a second message, which was really the reason Charly was answering so fast. "are you still coming to Tye's thing tonight or not."

Tye's thing was a show at the community space, doors at eight, and Brooklyn had said probably, then maybe, then stopped answering, because this essay was due Monday and she did not yet know what she thought. Charly wanted her there; Charly had helped Tye build the stage out of borrowed pallets and wanted witnesses. Brooklyn looked at the two articles open side by side on her screen and understood that her problem was no longer whether they disagreed, but how much weight each one could bear. The first had survived the slow examination of outside readers. The second had been posted publicly before any of that, its findings unchecked by independent experts chosen by a journal, which did not make it wrong, only unproven. She had nearly built her whole review on the unproven one because it was better written. That was a disincentive to trusting her own taste that she had never noticed before.

She drafted for an hour, and the drafting was strange, because the honest position turned out to be that she believed both articles partly. The measured one might be underestimating effects, and the confident one might be describing something real that checking would later confirm or trim. She wrote that the reviewer's task was not to referee a winner but to say what each piece of evidence could and could not support, and she left a sentence at the end admitting she did not know how much weight to give unpublished work, only that the difference in weight had to be named. It was the first time she had written an essay with a hole deliberately left in it. She kept expecting the hole to feel like failure and it felt more like a door she had chosen not to walk through yet.

The light had gone long and orange across the yard. Her grandmother had finished the beans and was reading a church bulletin with her glasses low on her nose. Brooklyn showed her the essay on the laptop, not for editing but just to have someone look, and her grandmother read the first paragraph and said, "You're not telling me what to think. Good. Too many people eulogize their own opinions and call it writing." Brooklyn laughed, surprised, and closed the laptop.

She texted Charly from the porch steps. "coming to Tye's. saving me a spot near the pallets." Then she went inside to find her other shoe.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
story:
Hayden had forty minutes before the bus came, and the library's computer terminals were all free, which almost never happened. He sat down at the one nearest the window, logged in with the temporary guest pass the desk had given him, and opened his phone to the video his grandmother had sent that morning: a flooded street, a man on a rooftop holding a sign that read WE ARE STILL HERE, and a caption claiming it was from a storm two days ago in a town three hundred miles from hers. Share if you care, the caption said. His grandmother had shared it to eleven people, including Hayden's mother, including the family group chat, including, he suspected, the retired pastor who thought weather was a personal message.

He wanted to reply to her, but the last time he had corrected something she forwarded, she had gone quiet for a week, and he didn't want to do that again. Robert, when Hayden showed him the video at lunch, had shrugged and said old people share stuff, it's not your job to police your grandma. Kamila had pulled the video up on her own phone, studied it, and said the water looked wrong somehow, too clean, and then said she had a study group and left before explaining what she meant. Between those two positions, Hayden had no position, which was the reason he was at the computer with forty minutes to spend.

He tried searching the caption's text first. That got him a fact-checking site that called the video miscaptionated, a word he had never seen, and the site wanted him to subscribe before it told him anything more. He tried searching the town name plus flood. He found a real flood, but from four years ago, and in the wrong part of town, and he couldn't tell if the rooftops matched. The man was reticent in every frame, mouth closed, sign raised, which made him readable as anyone's neighbor, anyone's victim. That was the trick of it, Hayden thought, that the image could transmute itself into whatever disaster was nearest to whoever was looking.

He was about to screenshot the paywall and send it to his grandmother with a question mark, which he already knew would land badly, when he remembered something Mr. Joshi had shown the class back in the spring. Mr. Joshi was the chemistry teacher who kept a shelf of old magazines in the lab and who, during a unit that had nothing to do with chemistry, had pulled up an image on the projector and dragged it straight into the search bar. Google added search by image in 2011, Mr. Joshi had said, his only complete sentence on the subject, letting users upload a picture or paste its link to find where else it appears on the web. Then he had assigned them a photo each and gone back to titrations.

Hayden paused the video on the clearest frame of the rooftop, cropped it on his phone, emailed the crop to himself, and downloaded it at the terminal. He dragged the file into the image box. The results loaded slowly, one of those library connections that seems to think about each page before deciding to deliver it, and behind him someone asked the desk if the printer took coins. The first results were stock-photo pages in languages he couldn't read. Then a news article from two years ago, from a different country, with the same man on the same rooftop, the same sign, the flood three years older than the caption claimed.

He leaned back. It wasn't just miscaptionated; it was recycled, the same man pulled out of one disaster and inserted into another like a prop. He saved the article, printed the page, and sat with the warm paper while he thought about what he actually knew. The storm in the caption might still be real. Floods happen in more than one place, and a video can be wrong about itself while the disaster it borrows for is genuinely drowning somebody. Kamila's instinct about the water and Robert's shrug and Mr. Joshi's single sentence were all true at once, and Hayden couldn't make them into one clean thing.

He composed a reply to his grandmother. He wrote three versions. The first said THIS IS FAKE, which he deleted. The second explained reverse image searching in a paragraph, which he also deleted, because she wouldn't read a paragraph and it would sound like a lecture. The third said, "Hi Grandma, I looked into that video and found out something interesting. Can I show you on Saturday? Bring your tablet." Then, because the library's parking lot had become a narrow isthmus of slush between the snowbanks and the bus would come whether he was on it or not, he gathered the printout, returned the guest pass to the desk, and waved thanks to the woman there who had found him the terminal in the first place.

Outside, he reread Kamila's last message and typed, "You were right about the water. The video is from two years ago." He attached the news article. Then he stood at the stop with his phone in his hand, watching the corner for the lights of the bus, and when his grandmother's reply arrived, a single thumbs-up followed by three question marks, he laughed out loud into the cold.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Lea's mother handed her the photograph in the parking lot, face down, the way you carry something that might spill. "You're putting him on the altar this year," she said. "You're the oldest grandchild. It's yours to do." Then she walked ahead with the foldable chairs, leaving Lea standing between the car and the park gates, holding her grandfather in both hands.

The park had been transformed overnight. Along the main path, families were building home altars called ofrendas, and Ms. Ma from the community center had stacked crates of orange marigolds by the fountain, handing them out in armfuls. Lea knew the flower part, sort of. Her grandmother had always said the cempasúchil was for guiding, though Lea had never asked exactly what that meant, and now there was no one left on that side to ask except an aunt in Monterrey who replied to texts three days late.

"Is that him?" Dani appeared beside her, peering at the photograph Lea had turned right-side up. In it, her grandfather stood in a driveway in 1987, squinting, holding a wrench like a man who had been interrupted mid-thought. "He looks like he's about to fix your whole family."

"He kind of was." Lea slid the photo into her jacket pocket. "I don't know if I'm doing this."

"Doing what, exactly? Carrying a picture forty feet?"

That was Dani's way of making a problem small enough to hold, and usually it worked. It wasn't working. Lea's mother wanted the photo placed tonight, on the ofrenda, before the marigolds went up, and she wanted Lea to say something. A few words. Her mother had been specific about the words: something about how the marigolds guide souls home, which Lea had repeated on the drive over and heard, in her own mouth, like a line in a play she hadn't auditioned for.

She'd spent two years being honest about the honesty problem. In chemistry, Ms. Ma had taught them that carbon could be an allotrope, the same element arranged one way as soft graphite and another as diamond, and Lea had thought at the time, with some private embarrassment, that she was also an allotrope of her family: same girl, different arrangement. At home she could sublimate the doubt, turn it straight from something solid into something invisible, no liquid stage. Here, in a park at dusk, with her mother arranging sugar skulls on a wooden table, the pressure and temperature were wrong for that. She felt metamorphic, pressed into a shape she hadn't chosen, and she resented it and wanted it at once.

Madeleine found her by the crates of marigolds, and they took an armful each, the scent sharp enough to follow without looking. "Okay, so my mom made me memorize the whole thing," Madeleine said, arranging petals on her family's altar a few tables down. "November first and second, Day of the Dead. The orange color and the strong smell, they're supposed to guide souls home. The dead can find their way back by following the flowers. My abuela claims she can smell them from, like, the other side. She says it like a threat."

Lea laughed, and the laugh surprised her. "My mom wants me to say that part. Out loud."

"So say it."

"If I say it, I have to mean it."

"Meaning it is optional," Dani said, arriving with a bundle of candles. "Saying it out loud at a party is not."

But it wasn't a party, exactly, and that was the thing nobody had warned her about. A man two altars down was playing a guitar badly and grinning about it. A kid in a skeleton mask was stealing orange petals one at a time and lining them up on a bench like evidence of a very small crime. A family had a whole plate of tamales out for a grandmother who was not, in any ordinary sense, going to eat them, and they were laughing about her appetite, and it wasn't disrespect, it was the opposite of disrespect, it was a version of grief that had somewhere to go.

Lea carried the marigolds to her family's ofrenda and set them in a jar. She took the photograph out and placed it at the center, under the paper banners, and looked at her grandfather's squint, and understood something small and usable: she did not have to decide tonight whether souls traveled or didn't. The tradition didn't require her verdict. It required the orange flowers and the strong scent and the photograph, and those things did their work whether or not she could certify the mechanism. She could hold the doubt and the marigold in the same hand. That was, she thought, the most grown-up position available to her, and she was almost sure it wasn't a cop-out. Almost.

Her mother came to stand beside her, not touching her, watching the photo. "Say it," she said quietly. "For me."

"Mom." Lea exhaled. "The flowers guide souls home. The bright color and the strong smell, they show him the way." She heard the words land somewhere between recitation and belief, and decided that was an honest address to give from.

Her mother nodded once, a small compressed thing, and put out her hand and straightened the photograph a degree. Behind them the bad guitar started a song everybody seemed to know except Lea, and the kid in the skeleton mask, having assembled a full row of stolen petals, looked up and down the path like a smuggler at a checkpoint, then popped one into his mouth.

"Spit it out," Lea called. "Those are for the dead, you little thief."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
story:
Aiden spread the printout on the kitchen table and weighted its curling corners with the salt shaker and his mother's mug, which still held an inch of cold coffee. The painting stared back at him: a woman in foliage, a thorn necklace cutting into her throat, a monkey tugging at the thorns, a butterfly pinned in her hair. Mr. Chea had assigned each student one Kahlo to analyze by Friday, formal analysis only, no biography, and Aiden had chosen this one because it looked the least complicated. That had been Sunday. It was now Tuesday night and he had written one sentence, which he had crossed out.

He opened his notebook and tried again. The palette, he wrote, is dominated by greens, delimiting the figure from the jungle behind her, except that the greens do not really separate her at all, because she wears green and the leaves press in on her from every side. He stopped. That was the problem with every sentence he produced: it argued with itself halfway through. He underlined "press in" and then wished he hadn't, because it looked decisive and he wasn't.

The doorbell rang twice, the impatient double-ring that meant Emerson. Aiden let him in, and Emerson came through to the kitchen carrying his own printout of the same painting, rolled like a baton, and a bag of the sour candies he ate when he was thinking. He sat down across from Aiden without being asked, which was how it worked between them.

"I'm stuck too," Emerson said, unrolling his print next to Aiden's so the two portraits lay side by side facing the ceiling like twins on a table. "Chea keeps saying describe what you see, but what I see is a lady and some animals, and then I start making things up."

"Which animals?" Aiden asked, mostly to delay working.

Emerson counted on his fingers. "Monkey. Butterfly. There's a bird thing on her chest, dead, I think. And a black cat." He leaned over the print, squinting. "The cat's behind her. It's peering over her shoulder. Like it's reading the painting over her shoulder."

Aiden had not even registered the cat. He pulled his laptop closer and searched, and the first result was a museum page that said, in a garrulous paragraph he had to read twice, that the black cat peering over her shoulder is usually interpreted as a symbol of bad luck and death. He read the line aloud.

"So it's the opposite of the dead bird," Emerson said, sucking a candy. "No, wait, it's the same. Death twice."

Aiden wrote the fact down carefully, word for word, because Chea had a rule that anything you looked up had to be sourced. Then he sat looking at it. The monkey, the sources said, was a symbol of tenderness, of the children she never had. The hummingbird, black and still, was death, or love, or both, and some pages said the thorns were Christ's crown and some said they were just pain, and Aiden began to understand why Chea had forbidden biography, because the moment you opened that door everything in the picture turned into a diary entry and stopped being a painting.

"Here's my problem," Aiden said. "Half the internet says everything means something and the other half says you should only talk about color and composition. And if I pick one, I feel like I'm lying."

"Then pick both," Emerson said, as if it were obvious, and reached across the table to slide the sugar bowl back toward the corner where it belonged, because Aiden's mother liked it there and would notice.

Aiden looked at the painting again, trying to see it the way he'd been taught in the unit on composition. The figure is frontal and symmetrical, he thought, almost icon-like, and the animals orbit her in a careful arrangement, monkey at her right, cat at her left shoulder, hummingbird at the center of her chest like a pendant. The symmetry wasn't peaceful. It was the symmetry of something pinned. He said this out loud, and Emerson pointed at the cat again and said that even the bad luck was arranged, orderly, on a leash of composition, and Aiden felt something click that he couldn't have written down yet.

He started a new page. Composition first: frontal symmetry, the animals placed in a balanced arc, the thorns creating a dark horizontal line at the throat that divides the face from the body. Color second: greens that refuse to delimit figure from ground. Then symbolism, and here he wrote more slowly, and the sentence he finally produced was: The cat peering over her shoulder, usually read as bad luck and death, is given the same compositional weight as the monkey's tenderness, so that the painting refuses to rank its own omens. He read it to Emerson.

"That's good," Emerson said. "It's not an answer, though."

"I know. I don't have an answer. I have a maybe." Aiden looked at the sentence again, testing it for cracks. "I think the maybe is the point. She hangs death around her neck and puts a death cat behind her and paints herself looking straight out at us, not scared. That's not a conclusion. It's more like an accusation. Like the whole painting is an indictment of the idea that suffering has to be private."

Emerson considered this while chewing. "Chea's going to love that sentence and circle the word indictment and write see me," he said. "He circles words he likes."

Aiden closed the notebook, then reopened it and added one line at the bottom, smaller: Uncertain whether the calm is defiance or numbness, and the essay cannot decide for her. He left it there, uncrossed out, because it was true. Emerson swept the candy wrappers into his palm and stood to throw them away, and Aiden slid his mother's mug toward himself and drank the last cold inch of coffee without meaning to.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
story:
Ms. Kowalski had taped two population pyramids to the whiteboard before first period, and by the time Sadie sat down, Antonin was already leaning across the aisle to claim the wide one. "I want Japan," he said. "It looks like a top-heavy chandelier. Easy essay."

Sadie got Niger. Her pyramid looked like a steep triangle, a cliff of young people narrowing to a thin ledge of old ones, and she copied it onto graph paper while the radiator clanked and Walker sharpened a pencil he had no intention of using.

"By Friday," Ms. Kowalski said, "you'll tell the class whether your country should be building more schools or more nursing homes, and you'll defend your answer from the shape of the pyramid alone. No copying conclusions off the internet. The shape is the evidence." She tapped Japan's chandelier with a knuckle. "Antonin will have an easy time of it. Sadie, you'll have to think."

Sadie had assumed it would be the other way around. A wide base meant lots of something, and lots of something seemed obvious, but obvious in which direction? She stayed behind when the bell rang and asked Ms. Kowalski which end of the pyramid was which, and Ms. Kowalski only said, "Young at the bottom, old at the top. Standard convention," and went back to her attendance sheet, leaving Sadie to work out the rest alone.

That was the trouble with Ms. Kowalski, who taught as though refusal to explain were itself the lesson. Sadie found Walker at lunch in the library, hunched over his own pyramid for Brazil, and slid into the chair opposite him.

"Look at this," she said, flattening her graph paper between his elbow and a carton of chocolate milk. "Niger. See how the base just flares out? It's the widest part by far." She traced it with her finger, down and out, the bars lengthening as they descended. "It's mostly children down there. The bottom of a pyramid is the young ages, so the shape itself is telling me there are more kids than anything else."

Walker squinted. "So nursing homes, then? Since the bars at the top are so short, there's barely anyone old to house."

"That was my first guess too," Sadie admitted, "but that's backwards. If you already have almost no elderly, you don't need new nursing homes. You need somewhere for all those children to go." She turned the paper sideways, so the triangle became a wedge widening toward the future. "Every one of those bars is a classroom of kids who are going to want a school."

"You're doing that thing," Walker said, "where you talk like the pyramid can hear you."

"It kind of can. That's the whole point of the assignment, isn't it? The graph is an argument." She thought of Antonin, who would stroll up on Friday, insouciant as ever, and announce that Japan needed nursing homes because his chandelier hung heavy with old people, and everyone would nod, and it would be correct, and it would have cost him nothing. There was something almost parasitic about the way easy answers lived off graphs that other people had bothered to build. She didn't say that out loud. Walker was already defensive about his chocolate milk.

That evening she tried to write the essay and stalled on the second paragraph. She could prove Niger needed schools; the shape said so, a wide base, a very large share of children, one of the highest birth rates in the world, which she had verified twice in the atlas because she wanted the number of the claim to be right even if she used no numbers at all. What she couldn't prove was whether a school built this decade would stand empty in fifty years, when today's enormous cohort of children had moved up the pyramid into those narrow top bars. The graph described the present with total confidence and the future only in outline.

She thought about her mother, who had gone back to school at forty and said it was the first decision she'd made that felt like it could emancipate her from waiting around for life to schedule itself. Her mother had planned for a future she couldn't see, on evidence that was really just a strong guess about a direction. Maybe that was all planning was.

On Friday, Sadie stood up with her graph paper and drew the steep triangle on the board. "Niger's pyramid has a very wide base and a very large share of children," she said. "So the answer to the assignment is schools, more schools, schools now. But I want to be honest about what I can't tell from this. I can't tell you what the pyramid will look like in fifty years. I can tell you where the need is today." She paused, then added, "And I think building for today's children is the right bet anyway, because a kid who gets a school becomes an adult who can read a graph like this one."

Antonin applauded with two fingers against his palm, which from him was practically a standing ovation. Ms. Kowalski wrote something in her book without looking up.

After class, Sadie stopped at the door. "What did you write?"

"A minus," Ms. Kowalski said, and then, almost smiling, "for the part you invented. The rest was all yours." She turned back to the pyramid still on the board, tapped the wide base twice, and said, "Leave it up for sixth period. Let them look at it."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
story:
Mr. Guo had written one sentence at the top of Sarah's draft, in pencil, underlined twice: "A thesis has to be arguable, a claim a reasonable person could dispute, not a fact everyone already accepts." Below it, circled, stood her own opening line: "The Amazon rainforest produces oxygen and is being deforested." She had carried the draft in her backpack for two days before bringing it to the café on Miller Street, where she spread it across the small table by the window and read the sentence again.

Riley slid into the seat across from her with a hot chocolate and looked at the pages upside down. "What's wrong with it? It's true."

"That's the problem, I think." Sarah turned the draft so Riley could see the penciled line. "He's saying I picked something nobody would argue with. Who's going to read my paper and say, no, actually, the rainforest isn't being deforested?"

Riley squinted at the page. "So he wants you to be wrong?"

"He wants me to be arguable." The word felt strange in her mouth, like a term she was trying to acclimate to, a coat that hadn't yet shaped itself to her shoulders.

Danae arrived twenty minutes late, as always, with her laptop already open and her elocution crisp from a morning of debate team practice. She read the draft while standing, one hand on the back of Riley's chair. "This isn't a thesis, this is a Wikipedia lead paragraph," she said. "You've got a topic. You don't have a position."

Sarah bristled. Danae had that effect, a truculent certainty that left no room for the person still figuring things out. "Fine. Then what's a position? That deforestation is bad? Everyone agrees with that too."

"Then go further. Deforestation is necessary. Deforestation should be taxed per hectare. Brazil's enforcement has worked better than international pressure. Pick something where a smart person on the other side exists." Danae sat down and started typing her own paper, a five-page assignment on voting rights that she would finish before her drink arrived.

Sarah pulled out her laptop and opened the folder of sources she had already collected, seventeen PDFs she had hoarded the week before without reading closely. She had assumed the paper would assemble itself from the pile. Now she went through them one at a time, and most of them fell away, because most of them only proved the fact she had already stated. Two did not. One argued that satellite monitoring had cut illegal clearing in Brazil more than any international agreement had. A second, from an economist in Lima, argued the opposite: that enforcement had shifted deforestation across borders rather than reducing it.

She sat with those two open side by side. Riley had gone quiet over her hot chocolate, and the café's afternoon crowd thinned to a cashier wiping the counter and a man reading a newspaper by the door. Sarah wrote in her notebook, crossed out, wrote again. Both sources were credible. Both could not be right, or maybe both were partly right, and she could not tell yet which, and she noticed that the not-knowing was not a failure in the paper but the actual reason to write it. She would have to choose a claim and defend it while the other evidence sat there disagreeing.

At four o'clock she typed a new first paragraph. Her thesis was that satellite enforcement had reduced illegal clearing in Brazil more effectively than international pressure had, and that the cross-border shift was real but smaller than the Lima paper claimed. It was a claim Danae might dispute, Riley might dispute, possibly Mr. Guo. She added a footnote to the enforcement study and a second footnote to the Lima paper, and then opened a new document for the bibliography and began alphabetizing, Chicago style, the way the handout showed, author, title, journal, volume, pages.

She looked up when the cashier turned the OPEN sign over. Riley was watching her. "So what's it actually arguing now?"

Sarah read the thesis aloud, once, listening to it the way Danae would, looking for the seam. Then she saved the file.

story:
Aaron had argued his way into the attic before the rest of the family finished unloading the car. His grandfather's house smelled of cedar and old coffee, and the box marked 1965 sat under the eaves exactly where Grandpa had said it would, behind a suitcase with a broken handle.

The whole thing had started in Ms. Virtanen's history class, two weeks from the end of term. She had asked them to investigate a local event using primary sources, and Aaron, who wanted more than anything to hand in something nobody else could, had remembered what Jaylen said at lunch: that Jaylen's grandfather and Aaron's grandfather had been arrested together at a draft protest in October of 1965, spent a night in the same cell, and been friends ever since. Jaylen told it like family scripture. Aaron wanted the diary to prove it.

He read it on the porch while his mother inside argued on the phone with an insurance adjuster, using words like indemnify, saying the company would have to cover the storm damage to Grandpa's roof and stop pretending otherwise. Somewhere in that conversation she promised to draft an affidavit, signed and dated, if that was what it took to be believed.

Aaron turned pages. October ninth: replaced the porch step, 4 dollars. October tenth: bowling, lost 6 dollars to Walter. October eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, nothing but weather and a note about the obstreperous rooster next door that would not stop crowing before dawn. October fifteenth: drove to Hazel's. Nothing about any protest. Nothing about any arrest.

He texted Jaylen a photo of the empty pages. "Never happened," he wrote. "It's right here in writing. He wrote down the weather every single day and he never once mentions a protest or a jail or you know, your whole grandpa." He felt the pleasure of holding proof, clean and dated, in his hand.

Jaylen arrived at the house twenty minutes later with his own phone held out, a scan of a clipping from the county paper, dated October fourteenth, 1965, showing two young men being walked toward a courthouse door. One of them was unmistakably Aaron's grandfather, twenty years old, hair longer than Aaron had ever seen it. "So it did happen," Jaylen said, "and your proof is worthless."

They took the diary inside to Grandpa, who was sitting by the window with his tea. He put on his glasses, turned the pages, and laughed, a sound that came out of him like something loosened. "An argument from silence," he said. "That's what your teacher would call it. You looked at what I didn't write and decided that meant it didn't happen. It happened. I just didn't write it down. I wasn't going to put that in a book my mother could find."

"But you wrote down the rooster," Aaron said. "You wrote down four dollars for a porch step."

"The rooster mattered to me that week," Grandpa said. "I was tired and I was furious about being in a cell and I wrote about the nearest loud thing instead. A diary is not a record of the world. It's a record of what one person noticed on one evening." He tapped the page. "And half the time, what a person notices is what he's avoiding."

Aaron sat with that. Nicole texted him then, asking if he'd found anything for the project, and he started typing "found out it never happened" and deleted it, then typed "found out my evidence was nothing" and deleted that too. The problem, he thought, was not that he had been wrong exactly. The clipping proved the arrest. But the clipping proved only the arrest. Whether the two men had been friends, whether the friendship lasted or was invented later at some reunion, none of that was in the diary or the newspaper, and none of it could be settled by silence in either direction.

"So what do I put in the paper I write?" he asked.

"Put both," Grandpa said. "Put the clipping and put the blank pages, and say what you actually know and what you don't. That's all any of us can do." He closed the diary and slid it across the table to Aaron, and Jaylen leaned in, and outside the wind moved through the cedars along the fence line.

story:
Elliot had read, somewhere, that you could decide what you felt by deciding how to act, so he spent the hour before Abigail arrived acting like a person who was merely tidying a living room. He moved the lamp, then moved it back. He collated the two remotes, the takeout menus, and the horror movie his cousin had sworn was the scariest thing ever filmed into a small ordered pile on the coffee table, and told himself the pile was preparation, not nerves. He was, he insisted to the kitchen in general, completely calm. His hands were shaking so mildly it could have been the refrigerator.

He had not told Abigail it was a first date, exactly. He had said movie night, and she had said sure, and in his account of events that was the same as both of them knowing. He was aware that this account was a work of fiction. He kept it anyway, the way you keep a jacket that no longer fits, because throwing it out meant admitting the shape of what was underneath.

Harlow had come over at four, uninvited in the manner of someone invited years ago and never uninvited, and was now lying across the couch Elliot needed for the date, eating the chips Elliot needed for the date. Where Elliot rehearsed things, Harlow simply happened to them. He had once slept through a fire drill and complained afterward about the noise. He was, Abigail said, the most phlegmatic person in their entire friend group, which she called a polity, mostly so she could hold votes about where to eat lunch and claim democratic legitimacy.

"It's a scary movie," Harlow said now, examining the case. "First movie night, and you picked the one that makes her grab your arm."

"That's not why I picked it."

"It's literally why anyone picks it."

Elliot took the case back. Here was the thing he had not said to Harlow: in Mr. Vargas's psychology elective last spring, on a day when the heat had melted everyone's attention into the desks, a paragraph in the textbook had snagged on him and stayed. In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge. The class had laughed at that, someone had said so fear works, and Mr. Vargas had moved on to the next slide without ceremony. Elliot had copied it into his notebook and then, ashamed of the copy, folded the page over.

He unfolded it now, in the kitchen, while Harlow's sister's car honked twice outside and Harlow peeled himself off the couch. "Her heart's going to be pounding from the movie," Harlow said from the doorway, hoisting his bag. "She won't know if it's you or the movie. That's the whole trick."

"It's not a trick if I know it's happening," Elliot said, and believed himself only partly.

After Harlow left, Elliot stood in the quiet and thought about the note, and about a night two summers ago when he and his father had crossed the swinging footbridge over the ravine at his grandmother's town, his father joking the whole way, and Elliot had felt his chest hammering, and at the far side a woman with a clipboard had asked if they'd answer questions for a trail survey, and his father had talked to her for ten minutes, flushed and cheerful in a way Elliot rarely saw. He had thought nothing of it at the time. Now he thought of it, in the half-dark of the kitchen, as evidence.

Abigail arrived at seven with her own bag of chips, which she set beside his as if completing a set. "So this is the famous living room," she said, and he said he'd never called it famous, and she said everything was famous now, that was just how talking worked. They put on the movie. Twenty minutes in, when the thing in the basement opened its mouth, she grabbed his arm, and did not let go, and he found that his own heart was going like a trapped bird, and he could not, honestly, could not tell which of them it was for.

"It's the movie," Abigail said during a quiet scene, still holding on. "Not you. I know the difference."

"Do you?" he asked, and told her, haltingly, about the two bridges, the interviewer, the men on the frightening suspension bridge who called her afterward more often than the men on the sturdy one, 1974, Dutton and Aron, the whole folded page of it. She listened with her knees pulled up. "So nobody knows which it is," she said. "That's what the study says. The body can't tell."

"The study doesn't say nobody knows," Elliot said. "It says the men who were scared thought they liked her."

"That's the same thing," Abigail said, and then the thing in the basement came upstairs and she pulled the blanket over both their heads, and underneath it, in the small blue light, she did not let go of his arm, and he did not move his, and neither of them said which it was.

When the movie ended she stayed through the credits, then gathered her bag and stood in the doorway with her keys, and said, "Same time Thursday?" and was down the steps before he answered. He locked the door and came back to the couch, where the blanket still held the shape of two people, and he put his hand on the warm place where her shoulder had been and left it there.

story:
Victor had taped the last wire down at eleven the night before, and now, in the gymnasium under fluorescent light, his capacitor rig looked smaller than it had on his workbench. Two aluminum plates faced each other across an air gap the width of his thumb, wired to a variable supply he'd salvaged from an old monitor. The poster behind him read, in letters he now found embarrassingly large, THE FIELD BETWEEN THE PLATES. At the sign-in table, Carlie had looked at the poster, then at him, and said only, "So you actually built it."

He had. What he hadn't done, entirely, was the math. He could compute the field strength at any point between two charged plates; Ms. Bianchi had drilled that until it was reflex, voltage divided by separation, uniform everywhere in the middle. Eight hundred volts across two centimetres gave forty thousand volts per metre, a number he liked saying to himself the way he'd once liked saying the names of dinosaurs, a private taxonomy of power. He'd designed the rig to reach higher. The dial on the supply went to three kilovolts, and on the drive to the school his father had asked, twice, whether that was safe, and Victor had said yes, and had not entirely known.

Stefan arrived midway through the first hour, hands in his jacket pockets, hair still wet from swim practice. He stood in front of the rig the way he stood in front of everything, weight on one hip, as if reserving judgment. "Show me," he said. So Victor dimmed the lights, chalk dust drifting through the beam, and cranked the dial. At fourteen hundred volts a faint blue thread leapt between the plates, snapped, and left a smell like a struck match. The small audience made the sound audiences make. Stefan didn't. He leaned in until the afterglow of the spark seemed printed on his glasses.

"Run the number," Stefan said. Victor did it on the back of his data sheet, pen pressed hard. Fifteen hundred volts, two centimetres. Seventy-five thousand volts per metre. "Now imagine your dial actually went where you wanted," Stefan said. "Three thousand across that gap. Hundred and fifty thousand volts per metre." He tapped the plate with one knuckle. "Here's the thing. Dry air at sea-level pressure breaks down and sparks at roughly three million volts per metre. That's the ceiling. Any field stronger than that across an air gap, you don't get a stronger field. You get a spark, and then basically nothing, the charge just dumps across." Victor looked at his dial, at the plates, at the black speck the spark had left on the aluminum, and felt the shape of his whole poster shift. He had been building toward a limit that wasn't the limit.

Ms. Bianchi came by before the judging, clipboard against her forearm. She asked about his methodology, and he answered, and then she asked the question he'd been dreading: what the maximum field in his design would be, and whether he had checked it against anything. He could have said yes. He had a page of calculations that looked like checking. Instead he heard himself say, "Stefan told me about breakdown this morning. Three million volts per metre in dry air. I hadn't looked at it before." She wrote something, and her face gave nothing away, and she moved on to the exhibit about tide pools.

He sat behind his table during the break, redrawing the chart. The sagacious move, he suspected, was to reframe the whole project around the ceiling itself, to map how close he could push the field before the air gave way. That was a real question, and it was honest, and it also meant admitting that the poster's big letters had promised something he hadn't understood when he printed them. Last spring he'd done the same thing with the history paper, turned in the version he'd planned rather than the one the sources had forced on him, and had gotten the A and had not felt clean about it. Carlie dropped into the folding chair beside him, unwrapping a granola bar.

"You look like your project died," she said. "It didn't. It told me something I didn't want to know." She chewed, watching the plates. "That's not death, then." He told her about the spark, the ceiling, the math he'd done in pen because pencil felt uncommitted. She listened with the attention she gave lab partners, which was to say completely and without mercy. "So rewrite the poster," she said. "You have an hour." "I don't have another poster." "You have tape and a marker. You've always had tape and a marker."

The judges came back at two. Victor's chart was crooked and his handwriting ran downhill, but the new heading, in smaller letters than before, said what the rig had actually taught him: HOW CLOSE CAN YOU GET. When the second judge asked what he'd do differently, he said, "Design the gap around the ceiling instead of pretending it isn't there," and heard Stefan, three tables over, exhale something that might have been a laugh. They announced winners at three. The name read aloud was not his, and Carlie's hand landed briefly on his shoulder, and Victor was already unscrewing the plates to try a wider gap, the marker still behind his ear, when the gym lights flickered once over the scoreboard.
