story:
The gym smelled of rubber matting and lime cleaner, and behind the front desk a fan pushed the smell in slow circles. Zoey had come in for her first shift, and Ms. Sun set a tablet on the counter between them, its screen already open to a form. "Onboarding," Ms. Sun said. "Everything's paperless now. Read the terms and conditions, check the boxes for consent, and sign at the bottom."

Zoey read. The employment agreement listed her wage, her schedule, the gym's right to change both. Below it sat a liability waiver, pages of it, warning about weights, wet floors, the negligence of other members. At the end, instead of a line for a signature, there was a button that said "Click to Sign." She pressed it once, lightly, the way she might test ice.

"Did that count?" she asked. "Signing. I just tapped a screen."

Michael was restocking the towel bin by the wall, and he stopped with a stack against his chest. He had applied for the same job and told her last week he'd take it if she didn't, so his attention had a sharpened edge. "It doesn't count," he said. "A signature is ink. My dad says anything digital can be faked. You could tap that button for me right now and nobody would know."

"That's why they call it consent," Ms. Sun said, and moved a stack of class schedules so their edges were square. She wanted the desk cleared by five, when the after-work crowd came through the doors in a wave that seemed to undulate across the weight room, one row of treadmills filling after another. "The form asks for your name and the last four of your social. The click is the signature." She said it the way she said everything, as settled fact, and walked off toward the studio.

Zoey was not sure settled facts were her job to accept. Between checking in two members and selling a day pass, she looked it up on her phone behind the desk: the ESIGN Act, passed in 2000, says a signature or contract may not be denied legal effect solely because it is in electronic form. She read the sentence twice. Not that electronic signatures were better, or safer, or that they couldn't be faked. Only that they couldn't be thrown out for being electronic. Michael's dad was half right, she thought; anyone could tap that button. But the law didn't promise the click was honest. It promised the click was binding anyway.

She told Michael during their break, out by the water fountains where the drinking made talking difficult and therefore private. "It's real. The ESIGN Act, 2000. A signature can't be denied legal effect just because it's electronic." He wiped his mouth with the back of his hand. "So when I clicked through my waiver, I actually waived the liability?" "You actually waived it." He looked at his own hands as if they'd done something without him.

Michael wanted the thing he thought he'd skipped, which was a way out. "Then it's a trap. Nobody reads the terms. They put thirty pages in front of you and the whole deal is designed so you click." Zoey conceded part of it; she had not read all thirty pages either, and the ones she'd read, she'd read fast, with a member waiting. But she didn't think trap was the right word. A trap had to be hidden. This was in the open and boring, which amounted to a different problem, one where the danger was her own impatience rather than anyone's deceit. She said something like that, less cleanly, and Michael said she sounded like a policy paper, and she said she'd take that as a compliment.

He wasn't entirely wrong, though, and she let that sit unresolved, because it was. She hadn't known about the law an hour ago; she could be missing something now. What she had was a position she could hold for the afternoon: the click bound her, the ink would have bound her, and the difference was smaller than the choice about whether to read. She went back to the desk and pulled up her own form again, the terms, the conditions, the liability she had released, and scrolled past her signature to the paragraphs she'd skipped.

Ms. Sun passed behind her with a crate of protein bars. "Slow shift," she said. "Good time to learn the desk."

Zoey kept scrolling. "It's a good time to read what I signed."

story:
Mr. Clarke had put a single question on the board before the bell rang: who pays when a plan goes wrong? Laurie copied it into her notebook, then, out of habit, wrote her own question beneath it, smaller, in the margin. She wanted to know whether her brother's hospital bill counted as a philosophy problem or just a bill, because the two were starting to feel like the same thing and nobody in her house would say so out loud.

Izak slid into the seat beside her with his helmet still clipped to his backpack, which was how he had been arriving all week, since the new one arrived in its glossy box. "Down Cooper's Hill in forty seconds," he said. "Ralph timed me. That's eight seconds faster than last month."

"You were careful last month," Laurie said.

"I'm careful now. I've got the helmet."

"Careful is not a thing you keep in a plastic shell." She said it more sharply than she meant, and Izak looked at her, surprised, because he knew about her brother, who had been careful too, in his way, right up until he wasn't.

Mr. Clarke called the room to order and arranged them into a debate neither of them had prepared for: whether the school should fund free helmets for every cyclist in the district. Izak argued for it with the confidence of a boy wearing one, and Laurie sat back and listened to the numbers pile up, the projected reductions in head injuries, the cost per student, the persuasive arithmetic of doing good cheaply. It all sounded correct the way a straight line sounds correct until you stand beside it and see it bend.

Then Ralph, who had been quiet, raised his hand. "Forty seconds," he said. "Eight faster. Since the helmet." He said it without malice, which somehow made it land harder, and Mr. Clarke asked him to say more, and Ralph shrugged and said only that Izak rode differently now, that everyone rode differently when they felt protected, that the safety changed the rider and not just the ride.

"That's called risk compensation," Izak said, flat, because he had looked it up two nights earlier, after the hill, after the strange lightness in his own arms. "People behave less carefully when a safety measure makes them feel protected, so the measure can deliver less benefit than predicted." He recited it like a confession he had memorized, and the room went quiet in the way rooms do when someone argues against their own side and means it.

Laurie wrote the phrase down. Underneath it she wrote her brother's name, then crossed it out, then wrote it again. She thought about the heuristic she had been carrying all year, the simple rule that more safety equals less harm, and how it had let her stop thinking at exactly the point where thinking was required. That was the trouble with shortcuts: they worked until they didn't, and the moment they failed was never marked in advance.

The debate turned to trade-offs, as Mr. Clarke said it must, because nothing worth arguing about was free. Someone wanted to monetize the program, translating saved skulls into saved dollars to prove it to the school board, and Laurie found herself objecting, not because the numbers were wrong but because they were being asked to carry a weight numbers couldn't hold. She did not sound petulant about it, or she hoped not; she said it evenly, that the counting was necessary and insufficient, that you had to count and still admit what the counting left out.

After the bell, Izak waited by her desk instead of leaving with Ralph. "I'm not going to ride slower just because you gave a speech," he said.

"I didn't give a speech. I asked a question." She closed her notebook. "The helmet isn't wrong. It's just not the whole answer, and I don't know what the rest of it is yet. Maybe slower. Maybe the hill at a different hour. Maybe nothing I've thought of." She was honest about the size of what she didn't know, and it felt less like defeat than she would have guessed.

He turned the helmet over in his hands, looked at the glossy shell as if seeing it for the first time, weighing something in his palms, and she watched him weigh it.

story:
Parker had the laptop balanced on the arm of the couch because the coffee table was buried under his mother's gardening catalogues, and he was trying to read a Washington Post article about warehouse workers for his history essay before dinner. The article was good, careful, full of numbers about injury rates, and he was halfway through copying a quote when Lexus dropped onto the cushion beside him and ate a handful of the popcorn Parker had been ignoring.

"Is that about Amazon?" Lexus asked, chewing. "Because my cousin works at one of those warehouses and he says the bathrooms are so far away you lose twenty minutes of pay just walking to them."

"That's exactly what the article's about," Parker said. He scrolled down. Then he stopped, because a thought arrived all at once, the way a smell arrives, whole and undeniable. "Wait. Who owns this paper?"

Tegan was lying on the rug with a chemistry book open on her chest, not reading it. She rolled onto one elbow. "The Washington Post? Some family, I think. Old newspaper families own newspapers."

Parker typed the question into the search bar. The answer loaded in two seconds, and he read it aloud before he could decide how he felt about it. "Amazon founder Jeff Bezos bought The Washington Post from the Graham family in 2013 for two hundred and fifty million dollars." The living room was quiet except for the radiator ticking and Lexus's fingers scraping the bottom of the popcorn bowl.

"So the guy who owns Amazon owns the paper that just wrote a hard article about Amazon," Lexus said. He sounded delighted, the way he always did when the world revealed itself to be crooked. "That's like grading your own exam."

"Or the opposite," Tegan said, sitting up now, the chemistry book forgotten. "Maybe he lets them attack him so it looks independent. Rich people do that. It's cheap for him, two hundred fifty million, I mean that's like a week of his money."

Parker read the number again. Two hundred and fifty million dollars for a newspaper that had been in one family for eighty years. He tried to picture the meeting where the Grahams signed it, some conference room, pens, and couldn't. What he could picture was his history teacher, Ms. Papadopoulos, who had assigned the essay and who had a reputation as a connoisseur of bad sources. She kept a laminated list on the wall titled "THINGS TO CHECK BEFORE YOU TRUST A PAGE," and the third item was "who pays for this?"

"That's actually on her list," Parker said. "Who pays for this. I always thought it meant, like, ads."

"Maybe we should ask her," Tegan said. "Or we could just argue about it here for an hour, which is what we'd do anyway."

Lexus had taken the laptop and was scrolling through other Post stories, hunting for something scandalous. He excoriated the paper's movie reviews, loudly and at length, because they had given three stars to a film he considered the worst thing made that year, and Tegan told him that had nothing to do with anything, and Lexus said it proved the whole operation was corrupt from top to bottom. Parker listened while chewing a cold piece of popcorn and found, to his surprise, that he could hold both ideas in his head at once: that the article might be shaped by its owner's interests, and that the article also contained injury-rate numbers from a government agency that Parker could go check himself in about four minutes.

He checked them. The federal numbers matched. He wrote that down, then wrote next to it, in smaller letters, "owner?" The word sat on the page looking back at him, less a conclusion than a door he hadn't opened.

"I'm not saying throw it out," Parker said finally. "I'm saying I don't know what I don't know. The facts in the article are real. Whether they chose those facts instead of other facts, because of who signs the checks, I can't tell from my couch."

"That's the most blasé revolution I've ever heard," Lexus said, reaching for the laptop again.

"It's not blasé, it's accurate," Parker said. "There's a difference."

Tegan had gone quiet, and when Parker looked over she had her phone out, tilted so he could see. On the screen was a picture of a different newspaper's front page, and above it a headline she had started typing for the school paper, the one she wanted to be editor of next year: LOCAL PAPER BOUGHT BY DEVELOPMENT COMPANY, and below it, "what changes and who decides?" She wanted the story, he realized, the way Lexus wanted the popcorn, which was to say completely and without apologies.

"Can I use your research?" Tegan asked. "The Bezos thing. It's a better example than mine."

"It's not mine, it's the internet's," Parker said, but he emailed her the link. Then he went back to the essay. He typed the sentence about the injury rates, and after it he typed a second sentence, that the paper's ownership was part of where the information came from, and after that he sat for a while with his hands off the keys, because he did not yet know what the third sentence should be. The radiator ticked. Lexus put his feet on the coffee table, right on top of a catalogue of rose bushes, and asked if anyone else wanted the last of the popcorn.

story:
The sled drills started the second week of August, on the flat stretch of grass between the softball diamond and the picnic shelter at Riverside Park. David had made the team as a midfielder, and the first weeks of training had gone well enough that the coach began testing who could push. The sled was an old metal frame with rubber mats stacked on top, and the rule was simple: two players, ten metres, as fast as possible. David pushed it with Malak on a Tuesday and they posted the third-best time on the squad.

On Thursday the coach changed it. He put the whole defensive unit on the rope harness, eight boys dragging the same sled across the same ten metres, and stood to the side with a stopwatch and a clipboard. The sled crawled. It moved, but slowly, and when the coach read out the time nobody said anything, because the number was worse than what pairs had done, and everyone knew it. The coach scratched something out on his clipboard and told them to run it again.

They ran it four more times that afternoon. On the fifth rep David planted his feet early, expecting the load to jerk against him the way it did when it was only Malak, and instead felt almost nothing, a soft resistance, as if the others had absorbed the work before it reached him. He looked down the line. Some of the boys were leaning into their harnesses. Two of them near the back were mostly upright, jogging, letting the rope go slack between their shoulders and their hands.

That evening he told Flavie about it while they sat on the hood of her mother's car outside the park, splitting a bag of sour candies. Flavie had done her season of track the year before and had quit, and she had opinions about teams. She said it sounded like people being lazy, and David said he didn't think it was that simple, because the two slack ones were the hardest workers in drills, and because he had caught himself easing off too, without deciding to. "Then it's not laziness," Flavie said. "It's something with a name, probably. Everything embarrassing about people has a name." She tossed him the last candy.

He found the name at the library on Saturday, in a chapter of an old book about groups that Mr. Lavoie, his retired neighbour, had pressed on him in June. The book described a French engineer, Maximilien Ringelmann, who had published in 1913 the results of an experiment with people pulling a rope: each person pulling in a group pulled less hard than the same person did pulling alone. David read the sentence three times. He photocopied the page. It was called the Ringelmann effect, the book said, and David said the name out loud once in the empty carrel, quietly, to fix it.

He wanted to take it straight to the coach. He had it folded in his pocket on Monday, and he almost handed it over before the session started, but Malak was stretching beside him and asked what the paper was, and David showed him. Malak read it, then read it again. "So it's not our fault," Malak said. "It's like a law." David said he didn't think a finding made it nobody's fault, and Malak looked at him like he was being difficult on purpose, which in a way he was, because he had spent Sunday turning the thing over and could no longer tell whether it excused them or accused them.

The coach noticed anyway. At Wednesday's session he split them up: he ran the sled with one boy at a time, then in pairs, then four, and wrote everything down. He never mentioned the engineer or the year or the study. What he did instead was stand behind the sled himself during the group pulls, calling out individual names, one after another, fast, so that each boy heard his own name inside the pull, and the times dropped. The sled moved like something being pulled by eight separate men who happened to be holding the same rope.

David understood the trick and also distrusted it. It worked because it made the group feel like a set of individuals again, each one watched, each one named, and that was fine for a Thursday in August. But the season was long, and the coach would not be standing behind them in October shouting names on a wet field in the last ten minutes of a match. Something would have to hold without the shouting. He was not sure what. He believed that people pulling together could pull hard, because he had felt it once already that summer, in the first scrimmage, when the whole midfield had moved as one wave; and he believed the finding, because the stopwatch had said it, twice, with the whole squad there to see. Both things were true and they sat side by side in his head without merging.

He tried to explain this to Flavie the following week, back on the car hood, and she was scathing about the coach's shouting method. "So his solution is to make you eight people who fear being caught slacking," she said, "instead of one team." David said he didn't think fear was quite the right word, and she asked him what the right word was, and he had to admit he didn't have one yet. She let him off with a shrug and changed the subject to her course selection, which was due Friday, and he listened, and it occurred to him that she had quit track for reasons she also hadn't fully named.

In the last week of August the coach ran the group sled once more, without shouting, as a kind of denouement to the conditioning block. He stood off to the side, arms folded, and let the eight of them pull in silence. The time was slow again, but not as slow as the first day, and afterward he read it out and said nothing about it, and neither did the players. Malak nudged David with his elbow and nodded toward the stopwatch as if it settled something.

Walking home across the park, David took the photocopied page out of his pocket, read it once more by the light of the lamp at the gate, and put it back. A man was pulling his dog on a retractable leash across the field, hauling it away from a garbage bin, alone, with his whole body. David watched him until the man and the dog disappeared behind the picnic shelter.
